title: Java & OOP
subtitle: Understand classes, objects, and how to structure Java code.
description: Learn classes, objects, interfaces, composition, collections, and exceptions through order and payment examples. You will use these concepts again when building Spring Boot applications.

lessons.title: Class, object & encapsulation
lessons.summary: Classes define fields and methods. Each object has its own state, and encapsulation controls how that state changes.
objectives: Distinguish classes, objects, fields, constructors, and methods.
Protect invariants with private fields and constructor validation.
Use final and immutable values where appropriate.
keyPoints: A class is a blueprint; each object is an instance with its own state.
Encapsulation keeps business rules in the methods that change state.
Validate constructor arguments before accepting an object as valid.
Final prevents reassignment; mutable referenced values still need protection.
practice: Create an Order with a private final BigDecimal total and an addItem method that rejects negative prices.
Invalid totals are rejected with IllegalArgumentException and total has no public setter.

exercises.prompt: Which statement best describes a class and an object?
options: A class is a blueprint; each object is an instance with its own state.
An object is a blueprint; a class is a copy of the object in memory.
Class and object mean exactly the same thing.
Each class can only have one object.
exercises.explanation: A class defines fields and methods. Each new expression creates an object with its own field values.

exercises.prompt: Why should Order.total be private and only changed through methods such as addItem?
options: So rules such as “total cannot be negative” are checked in one place.
To make the code run faster.
exercises.explanation: Private fields prevent callers from bypassing the methods that enforce business rules.

exercises.prompt: Complete Order: declare total as private final and reject negative totals in the constructor with IllegalArgumentException.
checks: Check for a negative total in the constructor
Do not expose a public total setter
exercises.explanation: Constructor validation checks the invariant before the object is returned to its caller.

lessons.title: Interface, polymorphism & composition
lessons.summary: An interface defines a contract. Polymorphism lets callers use different implementations through that contract, while composition connects objects.
objectives: Write an interface and multiple implementations.
Explain runtime method dispatch through an interface.
Prefer composition when reusing behavior does not require inheritance.
keyPoints: An interface describes the operations a caller can use.
Dynamic dispatch selects an implementation using the object’s runtime type.
Composition supplies a dependency instead of inheriting its implementation.
Use inheritance only when a subtype can fulfill its parent’s contract.
practice: Create PaymentGateway with BankGateway and FakeGateway implementations, then pass one to Checkout through its constructor.
Checkout can switch gateways without changing its payment flow.

exercises.prompt: Given PaymentGateway gateway = new FakeGateway(), which method runs when gateway.charge(100) is called?
options: FakeGateway.charge, selected using the object’s runtime type.
PaymentGateway.charge, because the variable is an interface.
Compilation fails because an interface cannot be a variable type.
exercises.explanation: Dynamic dispatch calls the implementation on the actual object, not a method chosen by import order or the variable’s declared type.

exercises.prompt: Checkout needs to charge a payment. Which design is most flexible?
options: Store a PaymentGateway received through the constructor.
exercises.explanation: Composition through an interface lets the caller choose a real or fake gateway without changing Checkout.

exercises.prompt: Implement FakeGateway as a PaymentGateway and record the most recently charged amount in lastAmount.
exercises.explanation: A fake gateway makes tests deterministic and lets them inspect the recorded amount without contacting a bank.

lessons.title: Collections, generics & records
lessons.summary: Choose List, Set, or Map for the way you access data. Generics check element types, and records keep data classes concise.
objectives: Choose List, Set, or Map for a use case.
Read and write generic types such as Map<Long, Order>.
Use Optional and records for explicit data contracts.
keyPoints: List preserves order, Set keeps unique elements, and Map associates keys with values.
Generics catch incompatible element types at compile time.
Declare an interface type and select an implementation separately.
Record components are final, but mutable component values still need defensive copies.
practice: Store orders in Map<Long, Order> and implement Optional<Order> findById(long id).
Missing IDs return Optional.empty() and callers handle the missing value explicitly.

exercises.prompt: Which structure is best for looking up orders by ID?
exercises.explanation: A Map associates an ID with its order. HashMap provides average constant-time key lookup.

exercises.prompt: Complete the method so it returns an empty Optional when the order is missing.
exercises.hint: Use the Optional factory method for an absent value.
exercises.explanation: Optional.empty() represents an absent order. Optional.ofNullable(orders.get(id)) is another concise option.

exercises.prompt: Write record OrderLine with String product and int quantity. Add a compact constructor that rejects quantity below 1.
checks: Declare record OrderLine(String product, int quantity)
Add a compact constructor without a parameter list
exercises.explanation: A compact constructor validates components before Java assigns the record fields.

lessons.title: Exception & resource lifecycle
lessons.summary: Exceptions separate error handling from the normal flow. try-with-resources closes files, connections, and streams when a block exits.
objectives: Handle failures without silently discarding their cause.
keyPoints: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared with throws.
try-with-resources closes resources even when an exception interrupts the block.
Preserve the original cause when wrapping an exception.
An empty catch block hides a failure instead of handling it.
practice: Read a product file using try-with-resources and report a missing file clearly.
Resources close reliably and the error identifies the file that could not be read.

exercises.explanation: IOException and SQLException are checked exceptions. IllegalArgumentException and NullPointerException extend RuntimeException.

exercises.prompt: Open BufferedReader with try-with-resources so it closes even when reading fails.
exercises.explanation: The original code skips close() if readLine() throws. try-with-resources handles cleanup on both success and failure.

exercises.prompt: What is the main problem with catch (IOException e) { }?
options: It hides the failure and may let the program continue in an invalid state.
It necessarily makes the program slower.
Nothing, as long as the file usually exists.
exercises.explanation: Handle the failure, let it propagate, or wrap it with context and its original cause. An empty catch gives the caller no indication that anything failed.
